Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore

Vignette:
Leilani had spent fifty years in operating rooms, her hands steady as she repaired the bodies of strangers. It was that same clinical confidence that had carried her through her own health crisis when, at seventy-four, a routine gallbladder surgery turned into a nightmare she could only partially recall. She remembered the first sharp wave of pain, then a nurse’s urgent voice, and then nothing—hours lost to a septic storm that nearly stopped her heart. What remained were flashes: the cold of an ambulance stretcher, a doctor’s eyes above a mask, the beeping of a monitor that seemed to slow. But the middle was a void, a stretch of time she could not retrieve no matter how many times she tried to replay it. Some moments stayed excruciatingly clear—the sensation of drowning in her own fever—and others were simply missing, as if someone had cut the tape.

In the months that followed, Leilani found herself doing something she had never done before: she started to ask why. Why had this happened to her, of all people? She had saved so many lives. She forced herself to think only positive thoughts—gratitude lists, affirmations stuck to her refrigerator—but the question never left. Worse, she no longer recognised the person looking back from the mirror. That woman had been certain, disciplined, unafraid of blood or bone. This new version was fragile, timid, and afraid of the very places she had once called home. She had lost her faith in medicine, in the system she had served, and in herself. The operating room, once her sanctuary, now felt like a stage set for a rerun of her own collapse.

Her avoidance was quiet at first. She cancelled her own annual physical, then rescheduled it, then stopped answering the clinic’s calls. A siren on the street sent her heart racing; she would step into a shop until it passed. Her divorce years ago had left her alone, and now she isolated herself further, turning down invitations from former colleagues and lying about feeling fine when her daughter called. The hardest moment came when a former scrub nurse invited her to a hospital retirement dinner. Leilani said she had already made plans. In truth, she had spent that evening sitting in her darkened living room, afraid that if she saw the hospital entrance, she would be sucked back into the blank space of her memory.

The consequences of these patterns accumulated slowly. She stopped going for her blood pressure checks, ignored a persistent cough, and no longer trusted any doctor—including, she realised with a start, the person she used to be. Her surgical identity had been so central to her sense of self that its loss left her drifting. She had become a woman who could not bear the sight of an ambulance, who could not walk into a hospital without feeling the floor tilt. Her relationships thinned; she could not explain to anyone why she had become so reclusive without revealing the shame she felt about her own weakness.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a letter from her primary care physician, informing her that she was overdue for a colonoscopy. She almost threw it away. But that night, lying awake, she realised she was more afraid of the blank spaces than of the procedure itself. She wanted to understand why she could not remember, why she could not move forward, and why the person she had been felt so unreachable. She hoped that by telling her story to a therapist, she might piece together the gaps and, perhaps, find a way to recognise herself again.
